The court can allow a delay in appropriate cases.The case goes before a Judicial Magistrate First Class. It is filed in the court that has jurisdiction over the bank branch where the cheque was presented for payment.What punishment can follow?A person convicted under Section 138 can face imprisonment of up to two years, a fine of up to twice the cheque amount, or both.The offence is bailable, compoundable and non-cognizable. context.title: What if a cheque bounces?
context.snippet:
A cheque may bounce for several reasons, including insufficient funds, account closure, stop-payment instructions or signature mismatches.
For instance, Kamal issues Priya a cheque for ₹50,000 which is dishonoured due to insufficient funds. The court initially presumes Kamal owed Priya ₹50,000 and issued the cheque only to repay that debt. Kamal can challenge this by presenting evidence that casts doubt on the existence of his liability to Priya. However, he does not have to prove his case entirely on his own; the court considers proofs from both sides before arriving at a conclusion. Legal timeline The payee can initiate proceedings under Section 138 only if the cheque was presented within validity period, usually 3 months from its date. If the cheque bounced, the payee, within 30 days of receiving information from the bank, must send a written demand notice to the issuer. The defaulter has an option to settle the payment within 15 days from the date of receipt of the payee’s demand notice. If payment is not made within the stipulated time, the payee might file a written complaint before the competent Magistrate within a month (30 days) after the 15-day notice period expires. The court may accept a late complaint if the complainant provides sufficient reason for the delay. The parties may also settle the case by mutual agreement as Section 147 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, permits such cases to be settled amicably. Further, the recipient may approach a civil court to recover the unpaid amount. For eligible claims, a summary suit offers a procedure to speed up the recovery of certain debts. Under the Limitation Act, 1963, a money-recovery claim usually must be filed within three years though the date from which this period begins depends on the nature of the claim.

context.title: Govt notifies grievance rules under VB-G RAM G Act, sets 15-day deadline
context.snippet:
The rules provide for designated grievance redressal officers at each level to receive, register, enquire into and dispose of complaints
The complainant will receive an acknowledgement with a registration number, date of receipt and designation of the receiving authority. The rules stipulate that an enquiry into a grievance must be completed within seven working days of its receipt, while the complaint must be resolved within 15 days. The designated officer can call for relevant records, documents, reports and electronic data from the authorities concerned and provide the complainant an opportunity to be heard, either in person or electronically, wherever necessary. Complaints not resolved within 15 days will be escalated to the next higher level under the mechanism established by the state government. Such cases will continue to be monitored electronically until their disposal. A district programme coordinator will oversee grievance redressal at the district level and ensure that complaints are addressed through the designated mechanism and digital infrastructure. The rules also provide for appeals against orders passed under the grievance redressal mechanism, in accordance with Schedule I of the Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) (VB-G RAM G) Act, 2025. The Act provides the statutory framework for the Centre's rural employment guarantee programme. The new rules lay down the institutional and procedural framework for addressing complaints arising from its implementation, including mandatory registration, time-bound enquiries and digital tracking. The ministry said the provisions are aimed at making grievance redressal more accessible and ensuring that citizens' concerns regarding the scheme receive timely attention.

If the Director accepts the complaint for resolution, he or she must notify in writing the complainant, the respondent, and the grantmaking agency. The notice must:

Contacting CRC about a complaint.

Both the complainant and the respondent, or their representative, may contact CRC for information about the complaint. The Director will determine what information, if any, about the complaint will be released.

Alternative dispute resolution.

The Director may offer the option of alternative dispute resolution (ADR) of the complaint filed with CRC. In such circumstances, the following rules apply:

(a) ADR is voluntary; consent must be given by the complainant and respondent before the ADR process will proceed.

(b) The ADR will be conducted under the guidance of the Director.

(c) ADR may take place at any time after a complaint has been filed under § 38.69, as deemed appropriate by the Director.

(d) CRC will not suspend its investigation and complaint processes during ADR.

## 1. Does the Dispute Qualify for the Commercial Division?

  

A breach-of-contract claim may belong in Supreme Court yet fall outside its Commercial Division. That distinction affects which court part will manage the case. Section 202.70 of Title 22 NYCRR sets the assignment criteria.

  

### Check the Claim Type and Monetary Threshold

Bronx County's ordinary threshold is $75,000. Punitive damages, interest, costs, disbursements, and attorney fees claimed do not count toward it.

| Claim | Commercial Division Treatment |
| --- | --- |
| Business contract claim | Eligible type if the threshold is met |
| Shareholder derivative action | No monetary threshold |
| Business entity dissolution | No monetary threshold |
| Commercial rent collection only | Excluded even above the threshold |

Commercial class actions also have no monetary threshold. For claims seeking equitable or declaratory relief, the rule measures the value of the action's object.

New York service of process carries a particular set of demands. Whether you need to serve legal documents to a party in the five boroughs or someone who resides in a small town upstate, it’s important to know how to [deliver effective service of process](https://www.abclegal.com/the-ultimate-guide-to-ensuring-proper-service-of-process). Developing a basis for understanding the key rules surrounding effective service of process can help you avoid unnecessary case delays and prevent legal matters from being dismissed for bad service.

## Service of Process: A Primer

If a plaintiff decides to sue another party, they must provide notice of the lawsuit and deliver all necessary legal documents. This notice allows the person being sued to understand what the claims are against them and what they must do if they choose to dispute those claims. “Process” is the term used to describe these legal documents, such as a summons or subpoena. “Service” is the term used to describe the delivery of these documents to the other party. People have a [constitutional right](https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/service_of_process) to know that someone has filed a legal claim against them. ## Filing a Complaint with CRC

***Filing a Complaint at the State or Local Level. ***Every recipient, except small recipients and service providers, must designate a recipient-level Equal Opportunity Officer. In addition, every Governor must designate an individual as a State-level Equal Opportunity Officer (State level EO Officer). These Equal Opportunity Officers are responsible for developing and publishing the recipient’s procedures for filing and processing discrimination complaints.

After a recipient reviews or investigates a complaint, a recipient must issue a written Notice of Final Action on a complaint within 90 days of the date on which the complaint is filed. If a complainant is dissatisfied with the recipient’s decision on the complaint, the complainant (or their representative) may file a complaint with CRC within 30 days after the date they receive the recipient’s Notice of Final Action.

Alternatively, if a recipient fails to issue a Notice of Final Action within 90 days of the complaint filing, the complainant (or their representative) may file the complaint with CRC within 30 days after the end of the 90-day period (in other words, within 120 days of the date the original complaint was filed with the recipient).

ultimate.title: 29 CFR 38.74 — Recipient's obligations when it determines that it has no jurisdiction over a complaint.
ultimate.snippet:
# 29 CFR 38.74 — Recipient's obligations when it determines that it has no jurisdiction over a complaint.

If a recipient determines that it does not have jurisdiction over a complaint, it must notify the complainant, in writing within five business days of making such determination. This Notice of Lack of Jurisdiction must include:
(a) A statement of the reasons for that determination; and
(b) Notice that the complainant has a right to file a complaint with CRC within 30 days of the date on which the complainant receives the Notice.
